answer.label: Not Michael Jordan — actually America’s Last Line of Defense
answer.authorDates: Satire and parody network of Facebook pages and websites · posted the line 24 January 2026
answer.sourceLine: Michael Jordan never said it. Snopes ↗ (Jordan Liles, 30 January 2026) rated the claim Originated as Satire and traced the wording to a 24 January Facebook post by America’s Last Line of Defense, a network whose flagship page carries the watermark “Nothing on this page is real.” Snopes adds that the post’s reference to the midterms “suggests that ALLOD may have recycled the fake quote from an earlier post,” so January 2026 is where the line is documented, not necessarily where it was first written.

source.excerpt: Michael Jordan says he can’t see why people would ever vote for a Democrat again. “All they want to do is protest and riot,” said the former NBA star, “Maybe they should try doing their jobs instead.”
trail: Snopes ↗ examined the claim on 30 January 2026 (reporter Jordan Liles), rated it Originated as Satire, and stated: “In short, Jordan never said those words.” It reproduces the originating post in full and links archived copies of the Threads and X reshares.

The wording came from a 24 January Facebook post by America’s Last Line of Defense. Snopes describes the watermark as “a small ALLOD logo with a very small ‘S’ label standing for satire, as well as the words, ‘Nothing on this page is real.’” Snopes’ “Originated as Satire” rating ↗ is defined as content described as satire by its creator that “was later stripped of those satirical markings as it spread online.”

This is a repeat performance by the same network. It put “If these kids can afford $8 cups of coffee, they can afford to pay their own student loans” in Jordan’s mouth in August 2024 (Snopes ↗, Labeled Satire), and an ALLOD subsidiary site had him wanting to “slap some sense” into Colin Kaepernick in November 2023 (Snopes ↗, Labeled Satire).

Nothing in Jordan’s documented public record resembles this. Quote Investigator ↗ returns no results for Michael Jordan at all, and his one widely cited political remark — the 1990 “Republicans buy sneakers, too” — he described in The Last Dance as “thrown off the cuff,” adding “I never thought of myself as an activist” (ESPN ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the opening of the fabricated post as Snopes transcribes it — not a Jordan statement. The post continued with an invented polling claim and a jab about the midterms; it is that midterms reference that led Snopes to suspect ALLOD had recycled the fake from an earlier post of its own.

sourceLink.text: Snopes: Did Michael Jordan say he doesn't know why anyone would vote for Democrats?

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted. The sentence is a fabrication written for a satire Facebook post in January 2026 and attributed to someone who never said it; there is no authored work, edition or publication date behind it to classify. It is certainly not public domain — the ALLOD post is recent and its authorship is unattributed — so treat the wording as unusable for reuse and cite the fact check, not the quote.

author.name: America’s Last Line of Defense
author.heading: About the source of the quote
author.metaLine: Satire and parody network of Facebook pages and websites · flagship page watermarked “Nothing on this page is real”
author.bio: America’s Last Line of Defense (ALLOD) is, in Snopes’ description, “a network of Facebook pages and websites that has historically labeled its content as parody and satire.” Its posts carry a small logo with an “S” for satire, and the page’s own Intro section reads: “The flagship of the ALLOD network of trollery and propaganda for cash. Nothing on this page is real.” Those markings routinely fall off as the posts are screenshotted and reshared — which is exactly what happened here, and what happened with earlier ALLOD fabrications put in Michael Jordan’s mouth about student loans and about Colin Kaepernick.

misattribution.heading: A recurring target
misattribution.intro: This is not a one-off. Snopes has repeatedly fact-checked political statements manufactured for Michael Jordan — most of them from the same satire network, and all of them false.

items.why: Snopes ↗ examined it on 30 January 2026 and wrote: “In short, Jordan never said those words.” The wording comes from a 24 January Facebook post by America’s Last Line of Defense whose watermark reads “Nothing on this page is real.”

Posts claimed Jordan announced he was leaving the Democratic Party because he “just can’t do it anymore.” Snopes ↗ rated it False and traced it to a now-deleted Facebook post; no reputable outlet ever reported such a statement.

Days before the 2024 U.S. election, X posts said Jordan had endorsed Donald Trump. A representative for Jordan told The Independent and the Daily Mail: “There is absolutely no truth to the claim that Michael Jordan has made an endorsement in the presidential election” (Snopes ↗).

“If these kids can afford $8 cups of coffee, they can afford to pay their own student loans” was an ALLOD meme posted 16 August 2024, shared more than 47,000 times in four days. Snopes ↗: Jordan “never made the statement.”

An ALLOD subsidiary site, Dunning-Kruger-Times.com, invented a phone interview in which Jordan wanted to “slap some sense” into Colin Kaepernick. The site’s own disclaimer reads, “Everything on this website is fiction” (Snopes ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: What Jordan has actually put his name to points the other way: a statement released 25 July 2016 opening “I can no longer stay silent,” alongside $1 million donations each to the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Institute for Community-Police Relations, as reported by NPR ↗.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Jordan
lead: Michael Jordan is an unusually good target for a manufactured political soundbite, and the reason is that he has spent almost his whole public life not making one. Snopes calls him “notorious for not speaking about politics”; the one episode everybody remembers — his 1990 refusal to endorse Democrat Harvey Gantt against Jesse Helms in North Carolina, reportedly with the line “Republicans buy sneakers, too” — he later described in The Last Dance as a joke made on a team bus. Because there is no long record of Jordan opining on politics, a reader has nothing to check a fresh “Jordan said” screenshot against.

The January 2026 version circulated while large demonstrations were under way against U.S. immigration enforcement, which is what gave “protest and riot” its bite. Snopes reports the quote spreading on Facebook, Threads and X, and says some commenters and Snopes readers “seemed to interpret the rumor as a factual recounting of real-life events.” The satire watermark that was on the original post does not survive a screenshot.
context.detailsSummary: What Jordan has actually said in public
detailsBody: The closest thing to a real Jordan statement on protest and policing runs in the opposite direction from the fake. On 25 July 2016, after the police shootings of Alton Sterling and Philando Castile and the attacks on officers in Dallas and Baton Rouge, Jordan released a statement through ESPN’s The Undefeated that began, “I can no longer stay silent,” and continued: “We need to find solutions that ensure people of color receive fair and equal treatment AND that police officers — who put their lives on the line every day to protect us all — are respected and supported.” He announced $1 million donations each to the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Institute for Community-Police Relations, saying the aim was to help “build trust and respect between communities and law enforcement.” NPR, reporting it, called the statement “a marked change for the NBA legend.”

On the sneakers line, Jordan told The Last Dance: “I said it in jest on a bus with Horace Grant and Scottie Pippen. It was thrown off the cuff.” He added: “I wasn’t a politician when I was playing my sport. I was focused on my craft. Was that selfish? Probably. But that was my energy.” That is the posture the fabricators keep writing over — a man who declined to be a political voice, recast as one delivering a partisan zinger.
context.pull: “In short, Jordan never said those words.” — Snopes, 30 January 2026

sourcesVerified.claim: Snopes, published 30 January 2026 by Jordan Liles, rated the claim "Originated as Satire", said "In short, Jordan never said those words," and traced the quote to a Jan. 24 Facebook post by America's Last Line of Defense whose watermark reads "Nothing on this page is real"; it also notes the midterms reference suggests ALLOD may have recycled the quote from an earlier post, and reproduces the post in full.

Snopes (Jordan Liles, 21 Aug 2024) rated "If these kids can afford $8 cups of coffee, they can afford to pay their own student loans" Labeled Satire; ALLOD originally posted the meme on Aug. 16 and it was shared over 47,000 times in four days; Jordan never made the statement.

Snopes (Jack Izzo, 5 Dec 2025) rated False the claim that Michael Jordan announced he was leaving the Democratic Party saying he "just can't do it anymore"; describes Jordan as "notorious for not speaking about politics" and traces the claim to a now-deleted Facebook post.

Snopes (Taija PerryCook, 13 Nov 2023) rated Labeled Satire the claim that Jordan wanted to "slap some sense" into Colin Kaepernick; it originated on Dunning-Kruger-Times.com, an ALLOD subsidiary, whose disclaimer reads "Everything on this website is fiction."

Snopes (Jack Izzo, 4 Nov 2024) rated False the claim Jordan endorsed Donald Trump in 2024; a representative told The Independent and the Daily Mail, "There is absolutely no truth to the claim that Michael Jordan has made an endorsement in the presidential election."

Snopes defines the "Originated as Satire" rating as indicating the claim stems from content described as satire by its creator and "was later stripped of those satirical markings as it spread online."

ESPN (4 May 2020) reports Jordan addressing the "Republicans buy sneakers, too" remark from the 1990 Helms–Gantt North Carolina Senate race in The Last Dance: "I said it in jest on a bus with Horace Grant and Scottie Pippen. It was thrown off the cuff," and "I wasn't a politician when I was playing my sport... I never thought of myself as an activist."

NPR (Nathan Rott, 25 July 2016) reports Jordan's statement released by ESPN's The Undefeated: "I can no longer stay silent... We need to find solutions that ensure people of color receive fair and equal treatment AND that police officers — who put their lives on the line every day to protect us all — are respected and supported," plus $1 million donations each to the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Institute for Community-Police Relations, to help "build trust and respect between communities and law enforcement."

Wikipedia's Michael Jordan article states he was born February 17, 1963 in New York City, and that in 1990 he declined to endorse Harvey Gantt, reportedly remarking "Republicans buy sneakers, too," confirming in The Last Dance that he made the comment on a team bus but intended it as a joke.
Quote Investigator has no article on any Michael Jordan quotation — a site search for "Michael Jordan" returns "Nothing Found."
